main_damage_causes: Total absence of Bill's HBP arc (Greyback attack, Fleur's declaration, hospital wing resolution) eliminates his only character-defining storyline and the relationship payoff that gives DH1's Shell Cottage sequences their emotional grounding.

Omission from GoF's third task and hospital wing scenes removes the foundational moment where Bill is established as someone who loves Harry and acts decisively for him, without which his DH1 role at Shell Cottage has no relational weight.

Theatrical cut of the Shell Cottage goblin-warning scene removes Bill's sole functional contribution to the DH plot — his curse-breaker expertise on goblin ethics — reducing him from an irreplaceable mentor figure to an uninvested bystander during the Gringotts arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 1 - Seven Potters / Privet Drive departure (Film Scene 4-5)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Bill is introduced at the Burrow in GoF as a fully realized character: cool, long-haired, dragon-hide boots, fang earring, relaxed confidence. By DH, he is a seasoned curse-breaker, an active Order member who left Egypt specifically to serve, and someone Harry has known and respected for years. His introduction in DH carries weight from that history.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film introduces Bill for the first time here with only a brief self-introduction ('Hello, Harry. Bill Weasley.') and a one-liner about his scars and Greyback. He has had no prior screen presence in any earlier film, so this moment carries no accumulated relationship weight. The audience meets him as a stranger.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Because the films omitted Bill from GoF's third task and hospital wing scenes, from OotP's Order scenes, and from HBP's Shell Cottage and Burrow sequences, he arrives in DH1 as a new face. The fraternal bond with Harry and the established Weasley-family dynamic that makes his role at Shell Cottage meaningful is absent. The audience has no reason to trust or care about him beyond the functional.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 1 - Shell Cottage arrival / Dobby's death (Film Scene 14-15)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Shell Cottage is Bill and Fleur's home, and Bill is a warm, capable host who takes charge: he tends the wounded, shows Harry where to dig the grave, manages the household under siege conditions, and serves as a trusted adult ally. His presence gives Harry a surrogate older-brother figure at a moment of grief and strategic crisis.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Bill appears briefly, observes Dobby's death from a distance, says 'Fleur's seeing to Ollivander. Anyone else need tending—' and then recedes. He shows no particular warmth toward Harry, takes no leadership, and the scene moves immediately to the Griphook negotiation without establishing any meaningful relationship between Bill and the trio.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Bill at Shell Cottage is a grounding presence who helps Harry process Dobby's death and transition into the Gringotts mission. The film reduces him to a background figure with a functional line, losing the elder-brother dynamic that gives the Shell Cottage sequence its emotional texture.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 1 - Shell Cottage parlor / goblin warning (Film Scene 17 - CUT SCENE)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Bill pulls Harry aside privately after Lupin's visit to warn him about goblin notions of ownership and the danger of breaking a promise to Griphook. This scene establishes Bill's unique expertise as a Gringotts curse-breaker, his genuine care for Harry, and his moral seriousness. It is a key moment of adult mentorship and foreshadows the sword-of-Gryffindor betrayal.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene was cut from the theatrical release per the non-theatrical exclusion note. Bill delivers only a brief, truncated warning in the parlor scene ('Listen, I don't know what you're up to, but I know goblins. If you've struck any kind of bargain with Griphook, you must be exceptionally careful to live up to it. If you don't... he won't be forgiving.') without the full explanation of goblin ownership philosophy, and the private, intimate quality of the book exchange is lost entirely.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The cut scene removes Bill's most important functional contribution to the plot: contextualizing goblin ethics and preparing the audience to understand why Harry's betrayal of Griphook matters morally and narratively. Without the full warning, the Gringotts heist and its aftermath lose thematic grounding. Bill's specialized expertise — the one thing that makes him irreplaceable at this story moment — is excised, reducing him from a meaningful mentor to a background family member.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 1 - Announcing Mad-Eye's death (Film Scene 7)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Bill returns from the battle, delivers the news of Mad-Eye's death with controlled grief, offers a toast, reasons through the question of betrayal methodically ('I know what you're thinking... But Mundungus can't have betrayed us'), and then immediately volunteers to accompany Lupin to recover Mad-Eye's body. He is composed, analytical, and courageous under pressure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Bill announces Mad-Eye's death flatly ('Mad-Eye's dead. Mundungus took one look at Voldemort and Disapparated.') and then recedes. The toast, the reasoning about the betrayal, and the volunteering to recover the body are all absent. He speaks two sentences and disappears from the scene's emotional center.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this moment to show Bill's leadership qualities: he manages the room's grief, performs rational analysis under emotional stress, and acts with courage by going back out into danger. The film strips all of this, leaving only the information delivery. His character voice — calm, competent, brave — is lost at the one scene where the film gives him a clear dramatic function.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 1 - Wedding reception (Film Scene 10)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The wedding is a culmination of the Bill-and-Fleur arc established across HBP: Mrs. Weasley's acceptance of Fleur, Fleur's devotion to Bill despite his scars, the family's joy. Bill dances with Fleur as the emotional heart of the celebration, representing hope and love persisting amid war. The book reader has watched this relationship develop from Bill's injury through Fleur's fierce declaration in the hospital wing.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Bill and Fleur dance briefly and are visible in the background. The scene has no dialogue or focus on them as a couple. The audience has no prior film investment in their relationship — HBP's hospital wing scene (Fleur's 'It would take more zan a werewolf') was not in the provided film corpus — so the wedding is emotionally hollow as a Bill-and-Fleur moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Because the films did not adapt HBP's key Bill-and-Fleur scenes (the injury, Fleur's declaration, the family reconciliation), the wedding carries none of the emotional payoff it should. For a film audience, Bill and Fleur are simply a couple at a wedding, not the culmination of a hard-won love story tested by violence and prejudice.

damaging_scenes.scene: Deathly Hallows Part 2 - Battle of Hogwarts, Great Hall (Film Scene 23)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: During the battle, Bill fights alongside his family and is present in the hospital wing aftermath attending to the dead. He is part of the collective Weasley grief over Fred. In the larger narrative he has been a full participant in the Order's resistance throughout DH.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Bill appears in the Battle of Hogwarts sequence (film scene 19, listed among those arriving at Hogwarts, and scene 23 in the Great Hall) purely as background. He has no lines, no individual actions, and no distinct presence in the climactic battle. He is visually present but narratively invisible.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A character who in the books has been an active Order operative, who moved his whole family into hiding, who served as Harry's host and counselor, is reduced to a face in the crowd during the saga's climax. The accumulated damage of his absence throughout the film series means there is nothing for the battle to pay off.

damaging_scenes.scene: Goblet of Fire - Third task / hospital wing (absent from film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Bill attends the third task with Mrs. Weasley as Harry's surrogate family. After Cedric's death and Voldemort's return, Bill is present in the hospital wing alongside Mrs. Weasley, visibly shaken and protective of Harry. He volunteers immediately to carry Dumbledore's message to Mr. Weasley ('I'll go to Dad. I'll go now'), showing courage, loyalty, and decisive action in a moment of crisis. This is the first time the audience sees Bill as a person who loves Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Bill does not appear in the GoF film at all. The hospital wing scene is absent. Mrs. Weasley attends the task alone (or not at all in the film's version), and the post-Voldemort-return sequence does not include Bill.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging absence in Bill's film adaptation. His GoF hospital wing role establishes his relationship with Harry, his decisiveness, his place in the Order, and his emotional bond with his family under genuine threat. Without it, every subsequent scene at Shell Cottage in DH lacks foundation. The audience never sees Bill choose Harry; they only see him hosting him.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Bill's injury and Fleur's declaration (absent from film corpus)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Fenrir Greyback mauls Bill, leaving him permanently scarred with wolfish tendencies. Fleur's declaration ('What do I care how he looks? I am good-looking enough for both of us') resolves the Mrs. Weasley / Fleur tension and establishes their relationship as genuine and tested. Bill himself, waking to find his personality essentially unchanged despite contamination, shows quiet courage. This arc defines Bill's character in HBP.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: HBP does not appear in the film corpus, and there is no evidence this arc was adapted. Bill's scars are mentioned in DH1 (he references Greyback in his introduction) but the dramatic context — the attack, the hospital scene, Fleur's speech, the family's reaction — is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is Bill's defining arc in the entire book series. It shows him as a victim of the war who loses something permanent yet retains his essential self; it redeems Fleur as a character; it moves Mrs. Weasley; it foreshadows the themes of bodily transformation and loyalty that run through DH. Its complete absence from the films means Bill has no arc whatsoever — he exists in DH1 only as a functional set piece, with scars that carry no earned dramatic weight.
